Counter-Strike 2 é simplesmente um jogão. A Valve conseguiu manter a essência que fez a franquia se tornar uma das maiores referências dos jogos competitivos, ao mesmo tempo em que trouxe melhorias importantes para a experiência.

O principal destaque, para mim, é a jogabilidade. CS2 continua sendo um jogo em que precisão, reflexo, estratégia e trabalho em equipe fazem toda a diferença. Cada partida pode mudar completamente em questão de segundos, e isso deixa o jogo extremamente emocionante. Não importa se você está jogando uma partida casual ou competitiva: sempre existe aquela sensação de que uma boa decisão pode virar o round.

Os tiroteios continuam sendo um dos pontos mais satisfatórios. A necessidade de controlar o recoil, conhecer os padrões das armas, dominar os ângulos e entender quando avançar ou recuar faz com que o jogo tenha uma curva de aprendizado enorme. É fácil começar a jogar, mas ficar realmente bom exige bastante prática.

Os mapas também são uma parte fundamental da experiência. Aprender posições, granadas, rotações e estratégias abre muitas possibilidades durante as partidas. Uma equipe bem coordenada consegue fazer jogadas incríveis, e isso mostra como CS2 vai muito além de simplesmente mirar e atirar.

Visualmente, o jogo também evoluiu bastante. A Source 2 trouxe melhorias nos gráficos, iluminação, partículas e diversos elementos visuais, deixando as partidas mais modernas sem abandonar a identidade clássica de Counter-Strike. As mudanças nas granadas de fumaça, por exemplo, adicionam novas possibilidades estratégicas e tornam algumas situações completamente diferentes do que os jogadores estavam acostumados.

Outro ponto muito legal é a competitividade. Poucos jogos conseguem proporcionar aquela tensão de estar em um round decisivo, com pouco dinheiro, poucos jogadores vivos e a partida dependendo de uma única jogada. Quando você consegue executar uma estratégia perfeitamente ou ganhar um clutch praticamente impossível, a sensação é excelente.

Também gosto muito da importância do trabalho em equipe. Comunicação, economia, posicionamento e tomada de decisões são essenciais. Mesmo sendo possível fazer boas jogadas individualmente, CS2 recompensa bastante quem consegue jogar pensando no time.

É claro que o jogo não é perfeito. Existem aspectos técnicos e situações que podem incomodar, além de momentos em que a experiência online pode não ser tão agradável quanto o jogador gostaria. Mesmo assim, esses problemas não mudam o fato de que a base do jogo é extremamente sólida e viciante.

No fim das contas, CS2 é um daqueles jogos que você abre para jogar algumas partidas e, quando percebe, já passou horas jogando. A combinação de competitividade, estratégia, habilidade mecânica e trabalho em equipe faz dele uma experiência que continua sendo muito divertida mesmo depois de centenas ou milhares de partidas.

The game is fun, but hackers and cheaters are ruining the game and making it unplayable, every two or three matches you encounter a cheater and it just ruins the game, devs need to up the anti cheat system.

The cheating problem in CS2 is completely out of control right now. It genuinely feels like you run into suspicious players way too often, and the current anti-cheat system just isn’t doing its job. Whether it’s blatant or subtle, the overall experience is constantly ruined by players who shouldn’t even be in the game.

What makes it worse is the lack of something like Overwatch from CS:GO. Back then, at least it felt like the community had some way of helping to deal with cheaters. Now, it just feels like you’re stuck hoping the system does something — which, most of the time, it doesn’t.

On top of that, the overall experience still doesn’t live up to CS:GO. Honestly, Valve should just bring CS:GO back properly, including 128-tick servers. The gameplay felt more responsive, more competitive, and overall just better. CS2, in its current state, feels like a downgrade in multiple areas.

Another major issue is performance. Many players are still experiencing significant FPS drops, inconsistent frame times, and overall worse performance compared to CS:GO, even on capable hardware. This makes the game feel less smooth and can negatively impact competitive play.

Network performance is also a concern. Net jitter, packet instability, and inconsistent hit registration continue to affect matches, creating situations where the game feels unreliable and frustrating.

In addition, there are still numerous graphical issues. Players frequently encounter visual bugs, rendering problems, lighting inconsistencies, texture glitches, and other graphical artifacts that hurt both immersion and gameplay clarity.

Right now, between the cheating issues, weak anti-cheat, performance problems, net jitter, graphical bugs, and missing features, it’s really hard to enjoy or recommend this game. Many players expected CS2 to be a clear upgrade over CS:GO, but for a significant part of the community, it still feels like a step backward.

I've been following it since it was in development (I stumbled across the game's dev blog as a link on the Starbound forums), it showed a lot of promise then, and it's continued to prove to be a really solid game.

Now, there's been a renaissance inspired by Stardew Valley and other life-sim games. I think this is great, as many of these games have unique twists and do certain things better than Stardew. But, I still think Stardew is really good, well rounded, and the perfect gateway game to the genre. And even though I've "completed" the game for now, I'm sure I'm going to come back to it when the next update drops or some friends want to do a multiplayer playthrough.

PS - If you're into board games, I'll also quickly say the Stardew Valley board game is a good time.

Stardew Valley sempre foi O JOGO cozy. E eu sempre me interessei por jogos cozy, mas tinha medo de investir neles porque meus notebooks sempre foram uma decadência. Ou, ao menos, era o que eu achava. Até que apareceu uma das promoções famosas da Steam e consegui comprá-lo por quase 10 reais.

Isso lá em 2020. O que foi conveniente, já que a pandemia bateu e eu tinha algo pra me entreter enquanto também fazia um TCC.

Desde então, Stardew Valley se tornou o jogo que eu ia e voltava algumas vezes em alguns anos. Depois do update 1.6, o lançamento de Good Luck, Babe da Chappel Roan, foi o que me motivou a voltar mais uma vez. Casei com a Haley, fiquei feliz com tudo que vi no update de 1.6, mas depois de uns meses jogando, coloquei de lado e fui me entreter com outros jogos.

Até que, há alguns meses, resolvi voltar de vez, mas dessa vez, para pegar a Perfeição pela primeira vez.

Como pode eu ter esse jogo desde 2020 e nunca ter visto a Perfeição antes?

Foi o que eu fiz. E não me arrependo. Peguei o save do casamento com a Haley, continuei de onde tinha parado. No final, eu senti que poderia ter terminado tanta coisa bem mais cedo, mas hoje eu entendo que não tinha como saber alguns detalhes que agora sei.

Não posso dizer que Stardew Valley é uma pérola no meio dos jogos, afinal, todo mundo conhece Stardew Valley, ora. Mas posso dizer, com confiança, que é um jogo que vai ajudar muita gente.

Mesmo que, no final, eu senti que estava passando pelo maior Edging ta minha vida só pra conseguir 10 milhões e comprar o bendito relógio dourado.

Stardew Valley é um jogo que eu considero muito divertido e relaxante. No começo, você recebe uma fazenda que está meio abandonada e precisa começar a cuidar dela. Aos poucos, você vai plantando, criando animais, pescando, explorando cavernas e conhecendo as pessoas da cidade.

Uma coisa que eu gostei bastante é que o jogo não obriga você a fazer tudo de uma forma específica. Você pode escolher o que quer fazer durante o dia e jogar no seu próprio ritmo. Também é legal conhecer os personagens, porque cada um tem sua própria personalidade e história.

Os gráficos são simples, mas combinam muito com o estilo do jogo. A música também deixa o ambiente mais tranquilo e combina bastante com os diferentes lugares e momentos do jogo.

Outra coisa que achei muito boa é ver a fazenda evoluindo. No começo ela está praticamente abandonada, mas conforme você trabalha, consegue deixar tudo organizado e construir uma fazenda do seu jeito. Isso dá uma sensação muito boa de progresso.

No geral, eu acho Stardew Valley um jogo muito completo e divertido. Ele mistura agricultura, exploração, aventura e amizade de uma maneira que não fica cansativa. É um jogo que dá para jogar tranquilamente e sempre encontrar alguma coisa nova para fazer.

9.5/10 game. I know I'm a bit late to review, and people probably won't see this, but here goes.
    A long time ago I played a game called Rune Factory frontier for the Wii, which was a very fun game. However, there were a lot of things about the game that I didn't like...Then, this game came out--and I heard a rumor that the developer was inspired by the harvest moon games. (The same people who made the rune factory games), and I knew I had to try it out. Fast forward to now, I've playing this game for years on the PC and even on the mobile version as well.
    What I loved was that Stardew Valley took a lot of what I liked about the rune factory games and made it... better. Even some of the issues from those games, Stardew somehow got rid of them with it's own unique story and game mechanics, and it really drew me in.
    As many of the people on here have said, there have definitely been some dark times in my life, where games like these was my only escape. I even played this game for a long time with my ex, and even though we split, I still see fond memories of her whenever I see this game in my library. Though, I'm still a bit hesitant to pick it up again whenever I see it, but I know one day I will return to my Stardew Valley--and everyone, the villagers, will be waiting for me! Who knows, I might return with friends as well :)

[h1]More than just a game.[/h1]

I've been playing Rocket League since around 2015–2016.

At some point, it stopped being just a game I played and became one of those things that quietly stayed with me through different parts of my life.

[b]Thousands of matches. Countless wins, losses, goals, saves, late nights, frustration, laughter, and memories.[/b]

Most of those matches are completely forgotten by now, but somehow the feeling of the game never left.

Rocket League has always had this strange magic to it. The concept is almost stupidly simple: cars playing football. Yet the skill ceiling feels endless. Even after all these years, there's still something satisfying about hitting the perfect shot, making an impossible save, or having one of those rare matches where everything just clicks.

I've watched the game change a lot over the years, for better and for worse.

And sure, I've hated this game more times than I can count.

But I always came back.

[hr][/hr]

Some games are fun for a few months.

Some stay in your library for years.

And then there are games like Rocket League, where you eventually realize that a small part of your life is attached to them.

[b]Rocket League is one of those games for me.[/b]

[h1][b]Rocket League[/b] is one of a kind, like no other.[/h1]

When we say [b]Rocket League[/b], people who isn't familiar with it probably go be thinking like [i]"haha, funny car soccer go brr",[/i] oh boi let me tell you it isn't just "a game" but it will also be draining your mental health if you're taking this beautiful sport very seriously. It's easy to learn, hard to master. Wanna learn cool mechanics? Even more difficult to learn and master. There's just so much you can do in this game, from controlling the ball on the ground to wall, dribbling in the air to the net etc, it's endless. Being a part of the team contributing simply by passing the ball to teammate, demolishing/bumping opponent(s) at the right timing, taking the opportunity to score, making great comebacks from 0-4, zero second goals and such.. it feels rewarding every time, those level of satisfaction is unbeatable. Not fond of playing as a team? Good news, there's [i]Duel Mode[/i] which is 1v1 so you only have to deal with an opponent and the demon in yourself. It's all fun and games until toxicity comes in. Somehow [b]RL[/b] is the only sports video game I love, and I don't even play any sports type in general. To be honest I don't like football either but I enjoyed watching some [i]RLCS[/i] scene on [i]Twitch[/i] live years ago. Watching the pros make amazing plays just leaves us in awe.

[b]RL[/b] is enjoyable in both Casual and Ranked, [i]Extra Modes[/i] is available too where it isn't regular ball or there's quirky power-ups to use against your opponents. You can play against bots as well if you just don't want to PvP. There is also a bunch of workshop maps where you can explore for more variety, some are very helpful for aerial training. However the learning part in general requires very lengthy time to practice just to improve at the game, ranging from hundreds to thousands of hours. Everyone will get better mechanically after each Season- so it is never easy for average players to return to [b]RL[/b] after a long break compared to most other games. Truth to be told, being in lower ranks is much more laid-back and less chaotic, when fun is all what matters. Those were really good old times. Believe me, once you've climbed to higher ranks it just doesn't feel as fun anymore. Every second counts, every small mistake is a golden opportunity for opponent to score, managing boost, the pressure from opponents.. each of these whole 5+ minutes match can definitely feel stressful. To maintain and grind the ranks you gotta keep on practicing from time to time. This doesn't sound so "haha funny car" anymore, right?

Not to forget that [b]RL[/b] actually have amazing list of anthem/music made by various artists. Often times it's not a bad idea to sit back and chill, listen to the music playing in the background at the main menu. The reason why I actually start playing this game was because of this one particular track, [i]Outbreak (feat. MYLK) by Feint[/i] used on one of the compilation video of [b]Dota 2[/b] clips back in year 2018. That song is fire! Occasionally been vibing to other songs such as [i]All I Need, LUV U NEED U, ROCK IT, Endgame, Flip Reset, just wanna luv,[/i] and many other classics too. They're all just sounds too pleasant to my ears!

I've got a total of 5707 Hours recorded, combined from [i]Steam[/i], [i]Epic[/i] and [i]Playstation[/i]. However, nearly half of the hours on [b]RL[/b] [i](roughly 2.5k hours)[/i] were for trading so the only hours I've truly played was around 3k+. Ever since Player-to-Player trading was removed on 5th December 2023, [b]RL[/b] starts to feel a little dull overtime. The item set collections I've obtained over the years somewhat feels worthless. However I still love [b]RL[/b] for its core gameplay, and there is no other to replace it. Even so with 3k+ Hours invested, am I good at the game? Nope, somehow been performing worse mostly. How about the people I've met along the way? I'm very grateful to have found long time friends through random matches and trading, though I've also made a few "enemies" in between for some reasons. The number of friends I've played together with all these years? Absolutely fun and memorable, including the moments we would just be raging at each other for trolling and making mistakes. Title: A Monument to Institutional Malice, Toxic Incompetence, and Betrayed Devotion: The Absolute Extinction Event of Among Us

I used to believe in this game with every fiber of my being. That unwavering, misplaced faith is now my deepest, most agonizing, and most humiliating wound. I didn’t just play Among Us during the 2020 pandemic lockdown golden age; I consumed it, breathed it, and sacrificed thousands of waking and sleeping hours to its colorful, deceptively simple spaceship corridors, treating its social deduction mechanics and frantic emergency meetings as a sacred second home. I spent years defending Innersloth's glacial update cycles, actively rationalizing their glaring server oversights, and aggressively dismissing the dark warning signs whispering through the community as the mere whining of disgruntled casuals. I was a foot soldier of a cult-like devotion, utterly convinced that this was a world crafted by independent creators who understood the fragile, beautiful bond between an indie developer and a passionate player base.

How intensely, unforgivably, and pathetically foolish I was.

What the public sees on the store page is a nostalgic, charming indie social deduction party game—a modest cartoonish masterpiece born from small-team work claiming to channel the ultimate psychological bluffing experience. But beneath that paper-thin, calculatedly deceptive facade lies a predatory, aggressively hostile ecosystem designed to exploit your time, weaponize your passion, harvest your free community moderation labor, and ultimately punish you for the singular crime of actually engaging deeply with public lobbies. The harsh reality of Among Us isn't a love letter to party gaming; it’s an institutionalized insult, a middle finger to anyone foolish enough to invest hundreds of hours into its structurally hollow and fundamentally broken framework.

Let’s pull back the curtain and talk about the unspoken horror that haunts the public lobbies of this game: the arbitrary, indiscriminate, and utterly cowardly ban hammer and chat censorship that targets the most dedicated players the moment they use basic deduction. For weeks, the veteran group chats whispered about it in paralyzing dread. Dedicated players—the exact backbone of the community, the people organizing logical deduction rooms, keeping custom game codes alive, and filling the community spaces with helpful strategy guides—would vanish overnight, or find their chat messages instantly star-filtered into absolute unintelligible gibberish. Their names were silently scrubbed, their accounts restricted, and their appeals locked behind an impenetrable wall of developer silence. I scoffed at the victims. I arrogantly told myself that I played completely legitimately, that hundreds of hours of honest sleuthing, meticulous task management, and raw social persistence would serve as my shield.

Then my inevitable turn came.

Mid-game, deep inside a high-tension emergency meeting where I had successfully tracked down the exact vent usage and alibi inconsistencies of a blatant teamer, the screen seized violently. The dreaded connection error warning flashed across the UI, followed instantly by a forced, unceremonious disconnect to the title screen. My hands shook uncontrollably as I scrambled to hit find game, enter a lobby, and was greeted by the most infuriating, gut-wrenching, soul-crushing notification: temporary suspension or chat restriction for daring to use harsh or direct logical callouts in a game entirely built around accusation and deception.

No warning. No specific rule violation cited other than automated keyword filters catching normal game banter. No human review whatsoever. Just an abrupt, summary execution carried out by a completely inept, automated moderation algorithm that apparently cannot comprehend the basic reality that a human being might actually want to play a social deduction game with passion and intensity. If you dare to actually play their game seriously, to push past the casual meme lobbies, and dedicate real, unbroken hours to mastering map routing, task speed, and psychological tells, their broken, hair-trigger security protocols automatically flag your communication as toxic behavior. They don't want a vibrant competitive social scene because they either haven't built a functional, stable infrastructure to sustain it, or they are utterly terrified of what veteran players discover when the illusion of wholesome casual fun is finally pulled back.

And when you turn to support for even a shred of recourse or human dignity? Prepare to crash headfirst into a brick wall constructed entirely of corporate apathy, cowardice, and automated responses. I poured my bleeding, broken heart into a meticulously written ticket—detailing my exact playtime, my absolute adherence to fair play, and my profound, heartbreaking disappointment. Within minutes, I was hit with the exact same robotic, copy-pasted wall of garbage text that every single restricted victim receives: "Your account action was upheld. This decision is final."

No appeal process. No human being willing to look at your case, check your match logs, or grant you basic respect. Just a cold, algorithmic middle finger from developers who happily take the cultural phenomenon, the active player counts, and the free social media virality of their base while treating us like disposable trash the moment an automated script misfires. The silence from Innersloth is deafening, pathetic, and entirely telling. They hide behind automated systems because facing the human wreckage of their broken chat filters and abysmal matchmaking design requires a spine they simply do not possess.

The technical and design state of the game outside of these tyrannical bans is an absolute disaster anyway, propped up by pure nostalgia and endless crossover merch. The public lobby experience is a chaotic, hyper-toxic mess dictated by trolls, leavers, and Discord cheaters who somehow bypass the very detection tools meant for honest players. Game balancing is practically non-existent, featuring bloated role additions that add artificial confusion rather than tactical depth. The repetitive gameplay loop quickly morphs from a casual throwback into an unrewarding, punishing, soul-crushing chore where nobody takes tasks seriously and everyone leaves the second they aren't assigned the Impostor role. Every single system feels half-baked, held together with digital duct tape and the nostalgic goodwill of players who desperately want it to succeed, only to be brutally kicked in the teeth the second they try to play a real match.

My account—complete with painstakingly unlocked cosmetics, hundreds of hours of irreplaceable memories, and genuine friendships forged in lobby chats—was crippled by automated censorship and broken matchmaking. All of it ruined, vaporized into the ether by developers who couldn’t care less if every single veteran social player walked away.

If you are a new player currently looking at this store page, reading the glowing mobile-port promises, or thinking about downloading this free-to-play trap: Stop. Do not install it. Do not give them your metrics. Do not invest your time, your energy, or your passion into a digital world that fundamentally despises its own community. Play literally anything else. Because if you actually stay, if you actually try to play public lobbies, and if you dare to care about the game too much, the only reward waiting for you is a communication ban screen and developers who refuse to look.

Among Us isn't just another failed multiplayer phenomenon; it is a meticulously constructed psychological trap for the devoted and an eternal monument to bad-faith development. Save your time, save your sanity, protect your peace, and stay far, far away from this toxic wasteland. It stands as a profound, unforgivable insult to anyone who ever believed that passion, time, and genuine emotional investment in a virtual social.

🚀 AMONG US — O JOGO ONDE SEUS AMIGOS VIRAM SUSPEITOS EM MENOS DE 30 SEGUNDOS

=== GRÁFICOS ===

🔲 Atari
🔲 144p
🔲 Parece desenho de guardanapo
✅ Simples e carismático
🔲 Gráficos de última geração

(O visual é simples, mas funciona perfeitamente. E, sinceramente, depois que começa a reunião, ninguém mais está prestando atenção nos gráficos.)

=== REQUISITOS ===

🔲 PC gamer
🔲 PC mediano
🔲 PC da batata
✅ Um computador que saiba clicar

(Se o PC consegue abrir o jogo, já está mais preparado que metade da tripulação.)

=== JOGABILIDADE ===

Você entra na partida com uma missão simples:

Fazer suas tarefas.

Parece fácil.

Até alguém morrer.

Aí o jogo muda completamente.

Antes:

"Vou terminar minhas tarefas."

Depois:

"QUEM ESTAVA COM ELE?"

"EU VI O AZUL."

"EU ESTAVA NA ELÉTRICA."

"MAS EU ESTAVA NO OUTRO LADO."

"ENTÃO É O VERMELHO."

"POR QUÊ?"

"INTUIÇÃO."

=== TRIPULANTES ===

🔲 Trabalhar em equipe
🔲 Fazer tarefas
🔲 Sobreviver
✅ Desconfiar de absolutamente todo mundo

Você pode estar tranquilamente fazendo uma tarefa.

Alguém entra na sala.

Você olha para ele.

Ele olha para você.

Ele sai.

Você pensa:

"Suspeito."

Parabéns.

Você acabou de criar uma acusação baseada em absolutamente nada.

=== IMPOSTOR ===

🔲 Discreto
🔲 Estratégico
🔲 Enganador
✅ "Eu não sou o impostor, confia."

O impostor precisa mentir, sabotar e convencer todo mundo de que é inocente.

O problema é quando ele começa a explicar demais.

"Eu estava na elétrica, depois fui para a medbay, aí passei pela cafeteria, depois voltei..."

Todo mundo:

"É ele."

=== REUNIÕES ===

🔲 Investigação séria
🔲 Trabalho de detetive
🔲 Discussão civilizada
✅ Tribunal internacional

Uma reunião pode começar com:

"Cadê o corpo?"

E terminar com:

"FOI ELE."

"PROVA?"

"EU SENTI."

"MAS EU ESTAVA COM VOCÊ."

"ENTÃO VOCÊ TAMBÉM É SUSPEITO."

Ninguém sabe o que está acontecendo.

Mas alguém será expulso.

=== ACUSAÇÕES ===

A lógica das partidas:

"Vi o vermelho perto do corpo."

"Então foi o vermelho."

"Eu vi o azul entrando."

"Então foi o azul."

"Eu estava fazendo tarefa."

"Então é o amarelo."

Em Among Us, estar perto de um crime já é praticamente uma sentença.

=== AMIZADE ===

🔲 Confiança
🔲 Amizade
🔲 Companheirismo
✅ "Eu confio em você."

5 segundos depois:

"FOI ELE."

Nada destrói uma amizade mais rápido do que uma reunião de emergência.

Seu melhor amigo pode passar 10 partidas te protegendo.

Na 11ª:

"Ele está estranho."

E você é expulso.

=== SABOTAGENS ===

🔲 Pequenos problemas
🔲 Incômodas
🔲 Estratégicas
✅ "TODO MUNDO PRA REATOR AGORA!"

Uma sabotagem transforma jogadores tranquilos em corredores profissionais.

Todo mundo correndo.

Ninguém sabe quem apertou o botão.

Alguém tropeça.

Outro começa a acusar alguém.

E o impostor está lá no meio pensando:

"Funcionou."

=== MAPAS ===

Cada mapa traz diferentes salas, caminhos e maneiras de criar situações suspeitas.

E não importa quantas vezes você jogue.

Sempre existe alguém que:

"Eu me perdi."

No mapa que você já jogou 400 vezes.

=== FATOR REPLAY ===

🔲 Baixo
🔲 Médio
🔲 Alto
✅ Depende de quantas vezes seus amigos conseguem te trair antes de você sair da partida

Cada partida pode ser completamente diferente.

Uma hora você é um tripulante inocente.

Na próxima, é o impostor.

Depois alguém te acusa sem motivo.

Depois você acusa alguém sem motivo.

Equilíbrio perfeito.

=== O VERDADEIRO AMONG US ===

Você entra na partida pensando:

"Vou jogar algumas partidas."

30 minutos depois:

"EU SABIA QUE ERA ELE!"

1 hora depois:

"COMO VOCÊ ACREDITOU NELE?"

2 horas depois:

"NINGUÉM AQUI SABE JOGAR."

3 horas depois:

"Mais uma."

=== VEREDITO ===

Among Us é simples, divertido e consegue transformar uma partida com bonequinhos coloridos em uma investigação criminal completamente caótica.

O jogo funciona especialmente bem com amigos, porque cada partida cria histórias diferentes.

Você pode ganhar por estratégia.

Pode perder por uma mentira muito boa.

Ou pode ser expulso porque alguém disse:

"Sus."

E todo mundo concordou.

It Takes Two — 10/10 ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

It Takes Two is one of the most creative and enjoyable co-op games I've ever played.

What makes this game special is how it constantly introduces new gameplay mechanics. Just when you think you've seen everything, the game surprises you with another completely different idea. Every chapter feels fresh, with new abilities, puzzles, challenges, and hilarious moments.

The level design is fantastic, and the game does an amazing job of making both players feel important. You can't simply let one player do everything—you actually have to cooperate, communicate, and sometimes save each other from disaster.

But beyond the gameplay, the story is surprisingly emotional. Cody and May's journey is funny, chaotic, and sometimes genuinely touching. The characters and their relationship give the adventure a lot more meaning than you might expect from a co-op platformer.

The visuals are beautiful, the soundtrack fits perfectly, and the attention to detail is incredible.

Most importantly, It Takes Two is the kind of game that creates memories with another person. The laughter, the arguments, the unexpected moments, and the feeling of finally solving something together are what make it special.

10/10 — A masterpiece of co-op gaming. ❤️🎮

It Takes Two is one of those games that managed to make me appreciate genres I normally wouldn’t enjoy. Its level design is exceptionally well-crafted, with seven completely different chapters, each offering its own unique gameplay ideas and atmosphere. What makes it even better is how well the story complements these changes, making every chapter feel meaningful rather than simply different for the sake of variety.

For me, the third chapter was the highlight of the game. The variety and creativity in its level design are incredible, constantly introducing new ideas and mechanics. The ending of the chapter was also one of the funniest moments I’ve ever had in a co-op game. My friend and I were laughing so hard that we literally couldn’t even control our characters anymore.

Overall, It Takes Two delivers an excellent co-op experience. My main criticism is that the puzzles and platforming are too easy. They rarely require you to really think or engage with the mechanics, which often made me breeze through the levels without much effort.

Even with that criticism, the creativity, variety, and sheer fun of the experience make it an absolute 10/10 for me.

[h2]Verdict[/h2]
✅ Recommended

One of the best co-op games on the market, and a great choice even for people who do not usually play games.

[h2]My history with the game[/h2]
I currently have 17.6 hours in It Takes Two on Steam.

I started playing it for the second time back in January, but I have not continued for a while because it is not always easy to find time with another player and finish a co-op game together.

Maybe I will finish this second playthrough one day, but even now I can say that this is a very good game.

[h2]Quick signals[/h2]
💸 Value: ✅ Worth it
🖥️ Requirements: ✅ Reasonable
🎨 Graphics: ✅ Beautiful and colorful
⏱️ Length: ✅ Good co-op campaign length
📖 Story: ✅ Simple, emotional, and fun
🎮 Gameplay: ✅ Excellent co-op variety
🐛 Bugs: ✅ No major issues for me

[h2]What I liked[/h2]

* It is one of the best games for two players.
* The co-op design is the main strength of the whole experience.
* Every section brings something new, so the gameplay does not feel repetitive.
* It is fun, creative, colorful, and very easy to enjoy with another person.
* The game works well for both gamers and non-gamers.
* It is a great choice if you want to play something together instead of just watching someone else play.
* The variety of mechanics makes the whole journey feel fresh.

[h2]What didn’t work for me[/h2]

* You really need another person to properly play it.
* Because of that, it can be harder to finish if both players do not have time.
* This is not the kind of game you can easily continue whenever you want alone.
* My second playthrough has been paused for a long time because of scheduling.

[h2]Is it an endless game? How long to beat?[/h2]
No, this is not an endless game.

It is a full co-op story campaign. I currently have 17.6 hours played, and depending on your pace, experience, and how much you explore or repeat sections, your playtime can vary.

[h2]Who will love it[/h2]
You will probably enjoy It Takes Two if you want a great co-op game, especially with a partner, friend, sibling, or someone who does not usually play many games.

It is one of those rare games that can be recommended to both regular players and casual/non-gamers.

[h2]Replay value[/h2]
Replay value is decent, especially if you want to experience it again with a different person.

For me, I already started a second playthrough, but I have not finished it yet because finding time with another player is the real challenge.

[h2]Final note[/h2]
It Takes Two is a very good co-op game and easily one of the best choices for two players.

I have not finished my second playthrough yet, but the game is creative, fun, polished, and enjoyable even for people who are not hardcore gamers.

Recommended to gamers and non-gamers alike.

Worth all the praise. One thing I'll say, though, is that it's not quite as beginner-friendly as people make it out to be.

If you're in a relationship with a non-gamer and you're thinking this might be the game that finally lures them in, I'm not going to say don't do it, but maybe keep your expectations in check and be mindful that it may not work.

It's not particularly difficult, but the game does assume both players have at least a fair understanding of how to use a controller: handling movement and camera simultaneously, working buttons and triggers together, etc.
It's not really a game where one player can carry the other. Progress requires both players to know what they're doing, especially during boss fights. If one person is mostly lost, you're going to get stuck.

That said, that's also what makes the game so much fun. The fact that you both have to work together to progress means neither player can just sit back and let the other do everything. You have to pull your own weight.

So if one of you has literally never held a game controller before, It Takes Two might not be the magical portal into gaming together you've been hoping for. Worth a shot, but be aware that you could easily end up giving up after an hour.

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]

[hr][/hr]
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h3]The Game[/h3]
[b]Gameplay[/b]
[i]It Takes Two[/i] lets you journey as a married couple, Cody and May, displayed in a split-screen format where you need to cooperate to progress. Each area focuses on a certain mechanic, with Cody and May granted different power that complements each other. The main focus of the game is on how you can utilize these mechanics to either help your partner or yourself to pass through the area.

For a co-op game, I found the experience to be smooth. I tend to have slight lag that can affect the gameplay experience a bit in co-op games since I usually play with someone on the other side of the world, but with this game, I didn't notice anything like that. There might be some input lag in the game, but they are not that noticeable, especially since the game has a lot of room for errors even when you are supposed to slam on a certain spot at the same time.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3791830096 

The different mechanics give a fresh take on the game. The gameplay might be boring, with you jumping around to avoid falling otherwise. Sometimes you will be armed with a weapon—other times you just have to make yourself smaller. There is even an area that changes the genre briefly into other genres. The game tries to mix up the playstyle a lot to keep things fresh. I never got bored playing the game due to that.

The game is a puzzle game at its core. A lot of the mechanics you have will be used to figure out how to progress. They are usually easy to notice, although there might be some that require you to use your brain a bit. Still, I found the difficulty to still be enjoyable for those who are not into games, though, unless they are trying to get 100% achievements. In that case, it's better to play it with someone who is into games since there is one achievement that requires you to climb on a tower which require some skill to do.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3791830190 

Some areas are very vast. While it can take a while to figure out where to go next this way, it was nice to explore the whole town and try to get lost. There are always some unique areas that you can visit or places where you can goof around. When you are done, you can always check the in-game marker to see where you need to go to progress the story.

The boss fights can be quite tough for those who are not into games, though. You need to avoid the boss's attacks, which either requires you to jump off between platforms or simply run to a certain area. However, the window to dodge might be smaller than you think. That being said, the game will still go on if one of you dies—you just need to mash a button while your partner tries to stay alive as best as they can, especially since the fight will reset if both of you die at the same time.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3793286784 

That being said, some areas can be boring. I hate the water area since it's hard to control the ship, and I also hate the garden area since there are a lot of fights there and I had to mash my button a lot just to attack the enemies. Moreover, each area can take a long time to finish, meaning that you must suffer for a while until you move to the next area.

The in-game scenery is superb. If you are one of those people who like seeing nice scenery in games, you are in for a treat. There is just a lot of variety in here, and the images look great if you take a screenshot of it.

[b]Length and Difficulty[/b]
I finished the game in 11.8h. I then replayed the game again so I could experience it as the other character until I finished it, which took me 21h. As for the difficulty, I found it to be quite easy, although you still need to think for a bit to solve some puzzles. There will be two brains thinking it out, though, so you shouldn't be having too much trouble.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
[i]It Takes Two[/i] is a high-quality game that can only be played with 2 people. Each person has a different ability in each area, leading to different playstyles. The scenery looks great, and the quality is top-notch. If you are looking for a nice game that can be played with another person, this game is for you.

[h1] Perfect to make, break a bond, or learn about CO-LLA-BO-RA-TION! [/h1]

It Takes Two is the game that introduced me to Hazelight Studios, and I was really thrilled to play it—and eventually finish it. A lot happened in between: I burnt a computer, waited about two years, and finally came back to complete it!

You can play as either May or Cody, a couple going through a pretty rough spot in their marriage and considering divorce. Their only child, Rose, can feel the growing tension between her parents and, as only a child with a pure heart and zero understanding of adult relationships and complex feeling would, assumes somehow it's her fault.

After finding Dr. Hakim's Book of Love, she accidentally transfers her parents' consciousness into two clay dolls. Now, May and Cody have to endure Dr. Hakim's rather questionable lessons while making their way through different areas of their home, learning about CO-LLA-BO-RA-TION and hopefully making amends along the way.

The gameplay is thrilling, but your experience may vary a lot depending on who you play with. It might be easier with some people and a real test of patience with others. Coordination, communication and CO-LLA-BO-RA-TION are key.

At times, the game can also feel surprisingly nostalgic. There are plenty of fun references to discover, beautiful and creative environments to explore, and mysterious achievements to hunt down. If you intend to play it more than once, though, I would recommend switching characters so you can experience the other side of the puzzles and keep things fresh.

With It Takes Two, Hazelight Studios created a bright, imaginative game with a great storyline, exciting gameplay, incredible environments, and, most importantly, a lot of heart. It's specially memorable for those of us who love a rich story wrapped inside a genuinely fun experience that we can share with someone we care about.

Is it a perfect game? No. But I do think it's a must-play, especially if you enjoy co-op games. It has its flaws, and some parts might test your patience more than others, but the overall experience is so creative and memorable that it's absolutely worth playing at least once.
